items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
items.content_html: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Bowel cancer “melted away” after immunotherapy, then stayed away
items.content_html: A short course of immunotherapy before surgery may offer remarkably durable protection for some patients with stage two or three bowel cancer. In the NEOPRISM-CRC trial, 32 patients with a specific genetic form of bowel cancer received pembrolizumab for up to nine weeks before surgery instead of the usual post-surgery chemotherapy. After nearly three years of follow-up, none of the patients had experienced a cancer recurrence, including those who still had small traces of disease after treatment.

items.title: 🔓 [WIRED] Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
items.content_html:
🎨 🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed. Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
items.content_html: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hubble Space Telescope may have found a planet born after its star died
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

A strange chemical signature in old Hubble observations may point to a planet that formed after its star had already died. Astronomers found unusually high levels of niobium around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832, suggesting some of the star’s expelled material may have assembled into a new gas giant. TESS data also hints at a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting just 3.7 million miles from the star.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists tested 5 natural compounds on cancer cells. One stood out
items.content_html: Five natural compounds, including curcumin and berberine, were tested for their effects on cancer cells and healthy muscle cells. All disrupted cancer cell energy production and pushed many of the cells into a non-dividing state, with curcumin producing the strongest overall effect. Curcumin also showed a relatively favorable safety profile, while some other compounds caused more toxicity.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice
items.content_html: Just seven strength-training sessions helped obese mice shrink visceral fat cells and reactivate molecular pathways involved in burning stored fat, despite no change in overall body weight. The findings suggest some benefits of resistance exercise may begin long before weight loss becomes visible, though the results still need to be confirmed in humans.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reprogram immune cells inside the body to fight cancer
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a way to create cancer-fighting CAR-T cells directly inside the body, potentially avoiding the slow and extremely expensive process of removing, engineering, and reinfusing a patient’s immune cells. Using a two-particle delivery system, the researchers sent CRISPR gene-editing tools and new cancer-targeting DNA specifically into T cells, where the DNA was inserted at a precise location in the genome.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
items.content_html: Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
items.content_html: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preserved.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Archaeologists may have finally solved a 100-year-old Florida mystery
items.content_html: Ancient pottery from Tampa Bay appears to have been made by migrant craftspeople who brought specialized Mississippian pottery-making knowledge hundreds of miles south. Remarkably, they even incorporated crushed fragments of older homeland pottery into new vessels, preserving a physical link to their past across generations.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Physicists just saw quarks make waves in the Big Bang’s primordial soup
items.content_html: Physicists at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider have captured the clearest evidence yet that quark-gluon plasma, the scorching-hot matter that filled the newborn universe, behaves like a true liquid. By tracking individual quarks as they blasted through the plasma, researchers saw them leave behind ripples, splashes, and swirling wakes much like a duck moving through water. The finding suggests this primordial “soup” is so dense that it can slow speeding quarks and respond collectively as a fluid.

items.title: [reddit.com] Physicist Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize for Antarctic neutrino observatory
items.content_html: Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded him 12 million Swedish kronor; the prize ceremony is scheduled for Dec. 10 [npr.org#2][physicsworld.com#1][nationalheraldindia.com#1]. Halzen proposed using South Pole ice to detect neutrinos in 1988. Completed in 2011, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice to record flashes produced when neutrinos collide with atoms. It detected the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond the solar system in 2013. Later observations identified a distant blazar as a source and detected neutrinos from within the Milky Way [theguardian.com#1][newscientist.com#1][astronomy.com#1]. Neutrinos can travel to Earth from distant, energetic environments while preserving information about their origins [bbc.co.uk#1][theguardian.com#1]. Halzen said he is working on a new proposal and hopes the Nobel recognition will help secure its approval [abcnews.com#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally see how nature moves energy so efficiently
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have captured key steps in a chemical reaction that helps nature transfer energy with remarkable efficiency. Ultrafast X-rays revealed how changes involving electrons and protons are closely linked to the rearrangement of surrounding water molecules. Because similar reactions drive photosynthesis and other energy-conversion processes, the technique could help scientists develop better catalysts, fuel cells, and flow batteries.
